synopsis: Embodied.cpp proposes a reusable C++ deployment stack for VLA and WAM models, with typed adapters, backbone execution, pluggable heads and configurable module scheduling. [e06, e07, e09] Its strongest reported configuration reduces HY-VLA latency to 0.37 and VRAM to 0.23 of its Python baseline while retaining 0.99 of baseline success. However, pi0.5 at 4-bit retains only 0.70 of baseline success. [e11, e13] The results demonstrate reported backend trade-offs, but missing hardware, task protocols and mechanism ablations limit conclusions about heterogeneous execution and control timing. [e16]

problem.text: The authors identify a deployment gap between trained embodied models and usable robot-side systems. Model-specific Python dependencies, sensor wrappers and backend assumptions complicate deployment across devices. They argue that an embodied runtime must support persistent, multi-rate control; low-latency batch-1 inference; and interfaces encompassing observations, actions and predicted futures.

contributions.text: An architecture-oriented comparison groups VLA and WAM systems by their inference structure, emphasizing that subgoals, predicted futures and buffered context should become explicit runtime objects.
A five-layer C++ runtime design separates input adapters, sequence builders, backbone execution, head plugins and deployment adapters, with supporting scheduling and backend abstractions.

Backend comparisons cover three VLA models with several precision configurations and two WAM deployments. These establish reported latency, memory and success trade-offs, rather than isolating individual runtime mechanisms.

inputs: Model-dependent images, language, proprioception and history
Optional force, tactile, IMU or simulator state through typed interfaces
Online sensor streams or offline dataset samples
outputs: Model-dependent discrete action tokens, continuous action vectors or action chunks
Predicted futures or intermediate control representations
Outputs passed through deployment adapters to robot or simulator software

steps.name: Adapt observations
steps.detail: Input adapters bring sensor streams and dataset samples into a typed embodied interface. The interface description accommodates multiple modalities, but does not specify their synchronization or model-specific preprocessing.

steps.name: Build sequences and execute the backbone
steps.detail: The proposed shared path places sequence builders before backbone execution. These are named architectural layers; concrete token layouts, sequence construction rules and per-model execution graphs are not supplied.

steps.name: Invoke model-specific heads
steps.detail: Head plugins accommodate the points where models diverge, including action generation and predictive computation. The architecture retains interfaces for future prediction and action experts without prescribing one world-to-action mechanism for every hosted model.

steps.name: Schedule modules at different rates
steps.detail: The design calls for explicit execution units, shared state or feature pools, and configurable refresh policies. Perception, predictive branches and action heads can therefore have separate execution cadences. No concrete refresh algorithm or synchronization protocol is given.

steps.name: Optimize device execution
steps.detail: The latency-first design calls for graph replay, buffer reuse, operator fusion, backend-specific dispatch and careful host-device transfers. These are presented as runtime principles; the evaluation does not separately measure their contributions.

steps.name: Bridge outputs to deployment
steps.detail: Deployment adapters connect runtime outputs to simulator and robot software stacks. The proposed stable boundary is intended to accommodate changing model internals and hardware while preserving embodied input/output semantics.

training.text: The proposed contribution concerns inference infrastructure. The paper specifies no new training objective, distillation procedure or training schedule for Embodied.cpp.
The VLA evaluation includes 8-bit, 6-bit and 4-bit C++ configurations, but does not explain the quantization algorithm, calibration data, precision allocation or whether adaptation was required.

inference.text: Learned prediction remains a property of the hosted policy or world-action model. Embodied.cpp supplies execution, state management and deployment interfaces; sharing a runtime does not imply sharing learned parameters across models.

Predicted futures are possible model outputs, while control commands reach the connected robot or simulator through adapters. The paper labels its reported success measurements as closed-loop evaluation, but does not identify whether the evaluated environments were physical or simulated.

results.setting: C++ configuration without a bit-width label; task suite, split, hardware and trial count unspecified.
results.metric: Normalized inference latency, success rate and VRAM
results.comparison: Each corresponding Python metric is independently normalized to 1.00.
results.interpretation: Reported latency is 52% lower and memory is 32% lower. Success is 1.02 times baseline, not an absolute 102% success rate; statistical significance is unavailable.

results.setting: 4-bit C++; same incompletely specified evaluation protocol as the other Table 3 configurations.
results.metric: Normalized inference latency, success rate and VRAM
results.comparison: Python: 1.00 for each metric. C++ without a bit-width label: 0.48 latency, 1.02 success and 0.68 VRAM.
results.interpretation: This is the table's strongest latency and memory reduction: approximately 2.70× speedup and 77% less VRAM versus Python, calculated from the ratios. It does not isolate scheduling or fusion benefits.

results.setting: 4-bit C++; benchmark, split, hardware and trial count unspecified.
results.metric: Normalized inference latency, success rate and VRAM
results.interpretation: Reported latency falls by 35% and VRAM by 62%, with 96% of baseline success retained. The absolute success rate cannot be recovered.

results.setting: 8-bit versus 4-bit C++; benchmark, split, hardware and trial count unspecified.
results.metric: Normalized inference latency, success rate and VRAM
results.value: 8-bit: latency 0.88, success 0.90, VRAM 0.41. 4-bit: latency 0.88, success 0.70, VRAM 0.30.
results.interpretation: The 4-bit configuration offers no reported latency improvement over 8-bit, reduces memory further, and retains substantially less success. Its 30% relative success loss versus Python qualifies the prose's broad success-retention claim.

results.setting: Author-described closed-loop evaluation; task, split, environment, hardware and trial count unspecified.
results.interpretation: Reported success decreases by 1 percentage point while memory decreases. No WAM latency measurement or video-prediction metric accompanies this result.

results.setting: Author-described closed-loop evaluation; task, split, environment, hardware and trial count unspecified.
results.interpretation: Reported success decreases by 2 percentage points with a reported 33.6% memory reduction. This is task-success evidence under an unspecified protocol, not evidence of video fidelity or verified physical deployment.

limitations.text: The evaluation omits task identities, data splits, success definitions, trial counts, uncertainty, hardware and absolute VLA latency. Normalization permits within-model ratio comparisons but cannot establish achievable control frequency or reproducible protocol equivalence.

Multi-rate scheduling and predictable control timing are central motivations, yet there are no refresh-policy ablations, latency distributions, jitter measurements or heterogeneous co-execution experiments. The feature matrix is the authors' coverage assessment, not a measured portability study.
The precision sweep is a useful configuration comparison, but cannot attribute gains to graph replay, fusion, buffering or scheduling. Python and unlabeled C++ precision details are also absent.

The conclusion says the revision quantitatively validates three VLA models and positions WAMs through architectural analysis, whereas Section 4 reports two numerical WAM comparisons. This internal inconsistency should be preserved when interpreting the revision.

reproduction.text: The title, identifier and all eleven authors match the catalog. The supplied title page identifies arXiv:2607.02501v3, dated 9 August 2026; the report uses the coordinator-supplied artifact provenance.

Reproduction requires exact checkpoints, backend and compiler versions, device specifications, quantization recipes, adapter configuration, task definitions, rollout horizons and evaluation seeds. Section 4 does not provide these details; in particular, the label Cosmos3 does not resolve an exact evaluated checkpoint.

A focused mechanism test would fix one checkpoint and precision, then independently toggle replay, buffer reuse and scheduling. Measure sensor-to-action latency distributions, memory and success on identical episodes. This is a proposed experiment, not a reported ablation.
The title page links a GitHub project. Its contents, availability and installation were not inspected, and no experiments were reproduced.

reasoning.text: The foundational-work category and technical-resource subcategory fit the runtime contribution, and architecture, prediction paradigm and quadrant are appropriately not applicable. A shared execution substrate does not establish a One Model WAM architecture. The specific conflict is the Training optimization & distillation subcategory: this paper describes inference optimization and quantized deployment, without a training-optimization or distillation method. The recorded snapshot is preserved unchanged.

discussionQuestions: Which runtime mechanism contributes most when checkpoint, precision, hardware and episode seeds are held fixed?
What state-versioning and synchronization rules prevent stale predictive features from producing temporally misaligned actions?
Which modules account for pi0.5's reduced success under 4-bit quantization, and would selective higher precision recover it?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block and arXiv version stamp
evidence.detail: The title and eleven named authors match the catalog; the version stamp reads arXiv:2607.02501v3, 9 August 2026.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–2, Section 1, deployment problem and three runtime requirements
evidence.detail: The introduction describes fragmented deployment stacks and motivates multi-rate execution, latency-first closed-loop control and extensible embodied interfaces.
The paper distinguishes four VLA and four WAM inference structures and identifies intermediate state and module timing as runtime concerns.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Table 2 and accompanying Section 2.2 discussion
evidence.detail: The authors mark Embodied.cpp as supporting all listed capabilities. Heterogeneous hardware means jointly using devices, rather than merely switching backends.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1, runtime overview and contribution list
evidence.detail: The named layers are input adapters, sequence builders, backbone execution, head plugins and deployment adapters. No sequence format or per-model graph is specified there.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 3.1, challenge 1; PDF p. 8, Section 3.2, principle 1
evidence.detail: The design calls for explicit modules, shared state or feature pools and configurable refresh policies, allowing perception, prediction and action components to run at different rates.
The latency-first principle lists graph replay, buffer reuse, operator fusion, backend-specific dispatch and host-device movement management.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 3.1, challenge 3; PDF p. 9, Section 3.2, project overview paragraphs
evidence.detail: The text describes typed sensor and dataset inputs, model-dependent action and prediction outputs, interfaces for action experts, a kernel warehouse, and adapters connecting to robots and simulators.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 3 caption and Section 4, VLA model evaluation
evidence.detail: Latency, success and VRAM are independently normalized to each model's Python baseline of 1.00. Latency is measured per generated action step before normalization; C++ configurations include unlabeled, 8-bit, 6-bit and 4-bit variants.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 3, pi0.5 row, 8-bit and 4-bit columns
evidence.detail: The 8-bit latency, success and VRAM ratios are 0.88, 0.90 and 0.41; the corresponding 4-bit ratios are 0.88, 0.70 and 0.30.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 3, GR00T N1.7 row, 4-bit columns
evidence.detail: The 4-bit latency, success and VRAM ratios are 0.65, 0.96 and 0.38.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 3, HY-VLA row, C++ and 4-bit columns
evidence.detail: Unlabeled C++ latency, success and VRAM ratios are 0.48, 1.02 and 0.68; 4-bit ratios are 0.37, 0.99 and 0.23.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 4, Cosmos3 rows, and WAM evaluation paragraph
evidence.detail: Python reports 49.00% success and 21.84 GB VRAM; C++ reports 48.00% and 19.49 GB. The prose identifies WAM metrics as closed-loop success and peak VRAM.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 4, LingBot-VA rows, and final WAM evaluation paragraph
evidence.detail: Python reports 100.00% success and 24.75 GB VRAM; C++ reports 98.00% and 16.44 GB. The authors state a 33.6% memory reduction.

Evaluation consists of backend and precision comparisons. It gives no named task protocol, split, hardware, trial counts, uncertainty, absolute VLA latency, WAM latency, quantization recipe or mechanism-specific ablation.
The conclusion describes quantitative validation on three VLA models and architectural positioning of WAMs, despite the numerical WAM comparisons in Section 4.
The paper provides the project URL https://github.com/SEU-PAISys/Embodied.cpp.
